disclaimer: Scoping-pass dataset built 2026-11-15 from Manitoba's Trapping of Wild Animals Regulation, M.R. 245/90 (current consolidation, in effect September 17, 2026), the 2026-2027 Manitoba Trapping Guide, The Wildlife Act, and related Manitoba regulations. PROVISIONAL research only - verify against the current regulation and guide before relying on any date, limit, fee, or rule. Manitoba seasons are set by fixed month/day in Schedule A of M.R. 245/90; the dates below are the 2026-27 instances (October-December dates fall in 2026, January-May dates in 2027). Seasons open at 12:00 a.m. on the opening date and close at 11:59 p.m. on the closing date (M.R. 245/90 s. 2).

sources.title: Fur Institute of Canada - Certified Traps list (updated July 22, 2026)
sources.notes: Manitoba does not incorporate the FIC list by reference in its regulation; the 2026-2027 Trapping Guide (pp. 25-26) reproduces the FIC certified-trap lists in two phases (Phase 1 mandatory, Phase 2 certified but not yet mandatory). Manitoba's binding device list is M.R. 245/90 Schedule B. The FIC list itself was cross-referenced during the Ontario pass.

license_summary.resident_open_area_licence: Resident (Open Area) Trapping Licence - $14.50 (2026-27 guide figure, incl. 5% GST and a Fish and Wildlife Enhancement Fund portion). Manitoba residents only: no trapping licences are issued to non-residents. The licence is valid in Open Trapping Area Zones 1-5, and a holder may trap in any OTA zone (the zone and Local Fur Council area are recorded at purchase for harvest tracking). Minimum age 12. First-time trappers must hold a trapper education graduate certificate (see trapper_education).
license_summary.resident_open_area_licence_treaty: Resident (Open Area) Licence - Treaty - free. For Treaty/status holders; available through Manitoba elicensing, Conservation Officer Service offices, and most First Nations band offices.
license_summary.registered_trapline_permit: Registered Trapline (RTL) Permit - $15.00 (2026-27). Issued through Conservation Officer Service district offices to the lineholder of a registered trapline section; the lineholder holds exclusive harvest rights on their line, and lines are awarded by competition (not sold or inherited). A person may not hold both an RTL permit and an open trapping area licence in the same trapping year (M.R. 245/90 s. 13), except that a landowner/tenant may hold an open area licence for their own land. Helpers may trap a line with the lineholder's written consent while the lineholder is actively trapping.
license_summary.youth_licence: Youth Trapping Licence/Permit (ages 12-17 on October 1) - free.
license_summary.trapper_education: Mandatory for first-time trappers: a trapper education graduate certificate from a course of at least 9 hours approved by the minister (M.R. 245/90 s. 4), or an equivalent certificate from another jurisdiction. Exam pass mark 80%; courses are usually 2 days or 3 evenings through the Manitoba Trappers Association. Hunter Education does NOT satisfy the requirement. Trappers who obtained a licence or permit before 1990 are exempt; anyone licensed after 1990 without a certificate must complete the course.
license_summary.special_trapping_area: Special Trapping Area (STA) harvest is by permit through Conservation Officer Service offices, with eligibility determined by the Conservation Officer for the area. Muskrat in the Southern Special Trapping District, the Northern Special Trapping District (guide only - see known gaps), Oak Hammock Marsh WMA, and Grant's Lake WMA is by special permit; any furbearer, black bear, or wolf in Game Hunting Area 38 is by special permit only (M.R. 245/90 s. 6).
license_summary.dead_wild_animal_possession_permit: Dead Wild Animal Possession Permit (Furbearer) - $10.50. Required to keep an accidentally captured furbearer; obtain one from a Conservation Officer as soon as possible after the capture. Subsequent accidental captures of the same species are turned over to the Conservation Officer Service and remain Crown property. Exception: open area trappers may not keep an accidentally taken black bear (except in the Northern Special Trapping District).
license_summary.export_permit: Export Permit - $21.00. A provincial export permit is required before shipping raw pelts out of Manitoba (Wildlife Branch, Winnipeg, 431-276-8352, or Conservation Officer Service offices). A federal CITES export permit (Environment and Climate Change Canada) is also required for bobcat, black bear, lynx, river otter, and wolf crossing international borders.
license_summary.vendor: Manitoba elicensing (manitobaelicensing.ca; new platform effective April 1, 2026), vendors, and Conservation Officer Service offices. 2026/27 resident trapping licences went on sale September 1, 2026. RTL permits are issued through COS district offices. All fees include 5% GST plus a Fish and Wildlife Enhancement Fund portion and are stated in the guide as subject to change.
license_summary.harvest_reporting: Harvest reporting is VOLUNTARY in Manitoba (contrast Ontario's mandatory report). Open area licence holders may complete the Trapper Harvest Survey (available until August 31, 2027) or the Furbearer Harvest Report Form / voluntary online questionnaire at manitobaelicensing.ca. Fur dealers must record all transactions and report by the 10th day after the reporting period; processors report quarterly.
license_summary.tagging: Tagging is narrow in Manitoba: a marten, fisher, or river otter taken in the Turtle Mountain Registered Trapline Section (the Southern RTL District) must carry a minister-issued tag or seal on the pelt or unskinned carcass before it is possessed for sale, bought, sold, or disposed of (M.R. 245/90 s. 12).
license_summary.rights_based_harvest: Status First Nations people may generally trap for food, traditional, or ceremonial purposes on reserve lands, wildlife management areas, provincial forests, areas of provincial parks where licensed trapping is permitted, unoccupied Crown lands, community pastures with permission, and private land with permission, without a provincial licence, and are not subject to AIHTS equipment restrictions. Pelts taken under rights may not be sold (sale requires a licence and full compliance). Safety and conservation rules still apply, and protected species may not be taken where prohibited (e.g., wolverine in open trapping areas).
license_summary.defence_of_property: Under The Wildlife Act s. 46, landowners and occupiers may take furbearers, black bear, and wolves in defence of property without a licence; the take must be reported to a Conservation Officer within 10 days (badgers taken this way must also be reported within 10 days), and pelts are not saleable except under permit.

species.notes: Arctic fox range in Manitoba is the Hudson Bay coast, and the season exists only in the two northernmost RTL districts. Leghold traps for arctic fox require pad inserts, laminated jaws, or offset jaws of at least 5 mm (M.R. 245/90 s. 7(5)). No bait within 10 km of the Hudson Bay coastline unless permitted, and no leghold trap or snare on land within 10 km of the coastline from September 1 to November 15 (ss. 6.1, 6.1.1).

species.notes: Black bear is big game under The Wildlife Act (Schedule A, Division 1) but is also taken under the trapping regulation. Firearm only - no traps or snares; a bear may not be taken in a den, and a female with cubs may not be taken (M.R. 245/90 s. 7(2)). Open area trappers may not keep an accidentally taken black bear, except in the Northern Special Trapping District. Any black bear in Game Hunting Area 38 may be taken only under a special permit (s. 6). A CITES export permit is required to export across international borders. The guide notes that when only a firearm is used to harvest an animal under a trapping licence, the activity is considered hunting.

verification.confirmation_notes: Every season date, quota, and area grouping was taken from Schedule A of the Trapping of Wild Animals Regulation, M.R. 245/90 (Manitoba Laws current consolidation, most current version as of November 15, 2026, in effect September 17, 2026, last amendment included M.R. 98/2026) and cross-checked against the season schedule in the 2026-2027 Manitoba Trapping Guide (MG-8691, Rev. 2026) - the two agree everywhere except muskrat in the Northern Special Trapping District (see known_gaps). Manitoba Schedule A uses fixed month/day dates only, with no relative dates; the 2026-27 instances place October-December dates in 2026 and January-May dates in 2027. The dataset's one relative date - the coyote hunting season's 'last day of February of the following year' (M.R. 165/91 Schedule H) - resolves to February 28, 2027 (2027 is not a leap year; verified by calendar check). Hunting rows for coyote and wolf come from M.R. 165/91 (in effect June 16, 2026), Parts 8 and 8.1 and Schedules G and H. Fees are the guide's published 2026-27 figures. Species designations were verified against The Wildlife Act Schedule A and M.R. 3/96; area and district compositions against M.R. 149/2001; licence eligibility against the Manitoba elicensing FAQ. Manitoba lies entirely within the Central Time zone, so every row uses America/Winnipeg (no split, unlike Ontario).
known_gaps: Muskrat, Northern Special Trapping District: the 2026-2027 Trapping Guide's season schedule includes the Northern Special Trapping District in the October 14 to May 31 muskrat group, but M.R. 245/90 Schedule A does not name the district for muskrat. The dataset follows the regulation (no Northern ST District muskrat row). Resolution: written confirmation from the Wildlife Branch, or a regulation amendment.

Muskrat, Gypsumville overlap inside Schedule A itself: Schedule A places the Interlake RTL District in the October 14 to May 31 group and also names the Gypsumville Registered Trapline Section (an Interlake section under M.R. 149/2001) separately with a spring-only March 1 to April 30 season. Both rows are reproduced as written; the specific spring-only row should be treated as governing Gypsumville. Resolution: Wildlife Branch confirmation.

Closed-area season rows (arctic fox outside the Barrenlands/Northern RTL districts; black bear in the OTA zones and Southern RTL District; river otter in OTA Zone 1; wolverine in the OTA zones) are modeled as season rows with null open/close dates and a CLOSED note, rather than in species-level notes only. The clone's season engine must treat a null-date row as 'no season in this area' and never as open.

Weasel is modeled as ONE species entry covering short-tailed, long-tailed, and least weasels, matching Manitoba's instruments (a single WEASEL line in M.R. 245/90 Schedule A). Ontario split its weasels into three entries. A product decision is needed if per-species weasel catch logging is wanted.

Striped skunk: verified absent - no season in M.R. 245/90 Schedule A, not designated a fur bearing animal in The Wildlife Act Schedule A or M.R. 3/96, and absent from the guide's season schedule (it appears only in the guide's fur-primeness chart). Its precise legal status (e.g., whether it may be taken in defence of property) was not verified from a primary instrument, so it is listed closed with that caveat.
Grey fox: not designated anywhere in Manitoba law (absent from The Wildlife Act Schedule A and M.R. 3/96) and given no species entry; recorded here so the omission is a decision, not an oversight.

Zone geography not transcribed: OTA Zone 1-5 boundaries and RTL section boundaries are defined by boundary descriptions and Plan 19319D under M.R. 149/2001, and Game Hunting Area boundaries under M.R. 220/86. A boundaries dataset is a separate task (the Ontario WMU-boundary equivalent).

Minor guide-vs-regulation wording differences: guide rule 31 includes muskrat in the leghold drowning-set rule, while M.R. 245/90 s. 7(3) names beaver, mink, and river otter only; guide rule 32's phrasing differs slightly from s. 7(4). The dataset follows the regulation text in both cases.

Fees are the guide's published 2026-27 figures and are stated to be subject to change; re-check manitobaelicensing.ca at build time. The responsible department is now Manitoba Natural Resources and Indigenous Futures (the guide's imprint); older material, including parts of the elicensing site, uses Natural Resources and Northern Development or Conservation and Climate.

Scientific names use modern standard taxonomy with scientific_name_verified: false throughout. The Wildlife Act Schedule A uses older synonyms for several species (Canis lagopus, Felis rufus, Felis canadensis, Lutra canadensis, Mustela vision, Martes pennanti, Canis vulpes, Felis concolor), noted per species where relevant.

aihts.models_note: This pass captured schedule structure and model counts per species from M.R. 245/90 Schedule B (243 named models plus 2 generic entries across 10 species); individual model names were counted, not transcribed. The Fur Institute of Canada certified-trap list cross-referenced through the 2026-2027 Manitoba Trapping Guide (pp. 25-26) is the July 22, 2026 edition.
aihts.note: Manitoba implements the Agreement on International Humane Trapping Standards through its own approved-device list, not by incorporating the Fur Institute of Canada list by reference: M.R. 245/90 s. 7(1)(e) restricts the ten Schedule B species to the devices listed in Schedule B (243 named models plus 2 generic entries; Schedule B last amended by M.R. 98/2026), and s. 7(1.1) allows any device for species not in Schedule B, subject to the general trap rules. The regulation never uses the word 'certified'; the 2026-2027 Trapping Guide (pp. 24-26) reproduces the FIC certified-trap lists in two phases - Phase 1 certified traps are mandatory (killing traps for beaver, fisher, marten, muskrat, river otter, raccoon, lynx and bobcat, weasel; restraining traps for beaver (cages), bobcat, lynx, wolf), while Phase 2 traps are certified but not yet mandatory (including coyote restraining traps; no killing trap is yet certified for badger), with the implementation year to be determined and at least three years' notice promised. Guide rule 29 matches the Schedule B species list. Three new certified traps were introduced for 2026-27 (guide, minister's message). The guide also carries a trap sales warning: vendors have sold non-certified traps as certified, and the onus is on the trapper. Approved power-assisted snares are listed separately in Schedule C (5 torsion springs, 4 breakaway devices, and a cam lock with teeth) for coyote and red fox.
trap_rules: Seasons open at 12:00 a.m. on the opening date and close at 11:59 p.m. on the closing date (M.R. 245/90 s. 2). Sunday trapping is allowed (s. 5). The trapping year runs September 1 to August 31 (s. 13(4)). The minister may extend a Schedule A season by written notice (s. 3.1).

Trap check: live holding devices must be inspected at least once every 72 hours (s. 8(1)); live trapping in defence of property must be checked every 24 hours (s. 8(3)). A live-trapped animal must be humanely killed immediately (s. 8(2)). The guide's responsible-trapping advice (not law) is to inspect live-holding devices daily in the early morning.

Only approved devices listed in Schedule B may be used for beaver, bobcat, fisher, lynx, marten, muskrat, river otter, raccoon, weasel, and wolf (s. 7(1)(e)); any device may be used for a species not in Schedule B (s. 7(1.1)), subject to the general rules.
No toothed or serrated traps; no hooks; no spring-pole sets; no leghold trap set in a tree or on a pole; leghold jaw spread must not exceed 23 cm (s. 7(1)).
110-size body-gripping traps (8 named models in the regulation) must not be used on land for any animal other than muskrat (s. 7(1.2)).

Leghold traps for beaver, mink, and river otter may be used only in drowning sets (s. 7(3)); no leghold traps for badger, red squirrel, weasel, or wolverine (s. 7(4)); leghold traps for coyote, arctic fox, and red fox require pad inserts, laminated jaws, or offset jaws of at least 5 mm (s. 7(5)).
Black bear: firearm only; not in a den; not a female with cubs (s. 7(2)).
Submarine traps may be used only for muskrat or mink (s. 7.1).

Common snares may be used only in the registered trapline area or the Northern Special Trapping District; exceptions are under-ice beaver snares in the open trapping area, power snares anywhere, and approved power-assisted snares (Schedule C devices) for coyote or red fox anywhere (s. 9). A snare on land requires a mechanical locking device that prevents the noose from expanding (s. 9(2.1)).
Traps and snares on land must be chained, cabled, or wired to a tree, grapple, heavy object, or stake (s. 9.1; the Victor Rat Trap is exempt).
Hudson Bay coastline: no bait within 10 km unless permitted or licence conditions allow (s. 6.1); no leghold trap or snare on land within 10 km from September 1 to November 15 (s. 6.1.1).

All traps and snares must be removed before the season closes (s. 10). Every trapped animal must be retrieved (s. 10.1(1)); hides and pelts must not be wasted, abandoned, or allowed to spoil (s. 10.1(2)).

No trapping in Birds Hill Provincial Park, Beaudry Provincial Park, parts of Pembina Valley Provincial Park, or ecological reserves; muskrat in Grant's Lake WMA, and any furbearer, black bear, or wolf in Game Hunting Area 38, only under a special permit (s. 6).

aihts.canada_wide: AIHTS in force in Canada since 1 June 1999 (Canada, the EU and Russia are parties; the US is not a party). FIC-certified traps mandatory per Phase 1 lists - killing traps: beaver, Canada lynx & bobcat, fisher, marten, muskrat (on land and underwater), otter, raccoon, weasels/ermine; restraining traps: beaver (cage), bobcat, Canada lynx, raccoon, wolf. Conventional steel-jawed leghold restraining traps on land are effectively banned for AIHTS species. Killing neck snares are NOT AIHTS traps and are not FIC-certified; provinces regulate snares separately. [R1 s.2a]

check_interval.live_holding: Live-holding devices: 72 hours; live traps for defence of property: 24 hours (secondary table).

canada_only.tenure: Registered Trapline system - 46 community-based RTL sections in the north (lines cannot be sold, inherited or handed down; awarded by competition/scoring) plus Open Area Zones and Special Trapping Areas.
canada_only.trap_id_requirement: None found - no trap owner-ID marking requirement in the sources searched (follow-up pass, Nov 17); identification runs through licence/tenure and pelt seals instead.
canada_only.royalty: No royalty currently payable - Wildlife Act s. 41 machinery survives, but the current Wildlife Fees Regulation (M.R. 31/92) prescribes fees only; the royalty schedule was removed in the 2016 amendments. [R2 Item 5]
canada_only.nuisance_route: Paid trapping generally prohibited - Wildlife Act s. 18 bars hunting/trapping for hire, gain or remuneration except as permitted. Narrow routes: (i) Targeted Predator Removal Program - a producer with a MASC wildlife-damage claim contacts the Manitoba Trappers Association, which assigns a trapper; trappers are paid time, mileage and equipment plus a per-wolf incentive; lethal only. (ii) Conservation Officer special permits for out-of-season property-protection harvest. Landowner self-help under s. 46 (no licence) must be reported to a CO within 10 days. [R2 Item 3]
